texts.moa:
MEMORANDUM OF ARGUMENT (FICTIONAL DEMONSTRATION DOCUMENT, NOT A REAL FILING)

Applicant: Mr. R. Example
Respondent: The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration

PART I - OVERVIEW

1. The Applicant seeks judicial review of a decision of the Refugee Protection Division that his refugee protection has ceased under paragraph 108(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, S.C. 2001, c. 27 (IRPA). The application is brought under section 72 of the IRPA and section 18.1 of the Federal Courts Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. F-7.

2. The decision is reviewed on the reasonableness standard: Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v. Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 at paras 10, 99.

PART II - FACTS

3. The Applicant, a citizen of India, was recognized as a Convention refugee in 2014. In 2022 he renewed his Indian passport to attend a family funeral and travelled to India for nine days.

4. The Minister applied to cease his protection under subsection 108(2) of the IRPA. The Member found that he had voluntarily reavailed himself of the protection of India and allowed the Minister's application.

PART III - ISSUES

5. Did the Member unreasonably find that the Applicant intended to reavail himself of the protection of India?

6. Did the Member breach procedural fairness by relying on evidence the Applicant was not shown?

PART IV - LAW AND ARGUMENT

7. The Member's reasons must be justified, intelligible and transparent: Vavilov, above at para 99. They must show that the Member grappled with the Applicant's explanation. Ibid at para 100.

8. Procedural fairness is assessed on the contextual factors in Baker v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), [1999] 2 S.C.R. 817 at paras 21-28.

9. Courts give weight to a tribunal's findings of fact: Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v. Khosa, 2009 SCC 12 at paras 59-62; Dunsmuir v. New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9 at para 47. That deference does not excuse reasons that ignore the evidence.

10. The Member treated the passport renewal as conclusive. Intent is a question of fact, and a short visit for a family funeral points the other way. The Member's approach was inconsistent with the principle that hardship must be assessed in context: Kanthasamy v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 SCC 61 at paras 21-23, 33.

11. A recent decision of this Court confirms that a bare finding of reavailment, without reasons on intent, cannot stand: Smith v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2021 FC 999 at para 14. Subsection 108(1) of the IRPA does not make a passport renewal conclusive.

PART V - ORDER SOUGHT

12. The Applicant asks that the decision be set aside and the matter returned to a differently constituted panel.

intro.title: Welcome to iLit
intro.text: iLit is a website for researching Canadian immigration case law. It gathers public court and tribunal decisions into one library, makes them searchable, and shows each decision in a clean reader with the cases and statutes it relies on beside the text. It runs in an ordinary browser, with nothing to install. Each step says what is about to happen; press Next to see it done. The bar at the bottom has Next, Back, Skip section and Exit.

intro.title: The library today
intro.text: These figures are read from the database when the page opens: the decisions in the library, the citations found in them, and the Federal Court immigration files held with their full docket history.

intro.title: Why it was built
intro.text: Immigration litigation is growing, and much of what would help is already public but scattered: decisions, docket entries and the authorities they cite sit on different websites, and the links between them are not shown. iLit brings that record together and connects it. It is a research aid; it does not give legal advice or predict results.

intro.title: Who it is for
intro.text: It is designed for the Canada Border Services Agency's immigration litigation work, mainly the Hearings and Litigation Division. That is a design target, not an endorsement: the Agency has not adopted it.

intro.title: How it works
intro.text: Every decision follows the same path. It is collected from the public court and tribunal websites with its source link, split into numbered paragraphs, and read by fixed rules that find the citations, statute references, judge, outcome and case type. The same decision always gives the same result, and no AI is called when you use the site.
intro.say: How it works explains where the decisions come from and how everything beside them is worked out. Next opens it.

intro.title: How each piece is worked out
intro.text: Citations, statutes, outcomes, case types and judges each have their own rules, described here with what they can and cannot do yet. Where the rules cannot tell, the site says so instead of guessing.

steps.title: Research
steps.text: Research is where most work starts. One box takes a case name, a citation such as 2019 SCC 65, or words from the reasons. Filters narrow any search.
steps.leadText: A short tour of the main features, starting with Research.

steps.title: A plain search
steps.text: Every decision whose reasons use those words is listed with its court, date, judge, outcome and case type, and how often other decisions cite it.
steps.say: A plain search: best interests of the child.

steps.title: A legal question in plain words
steps.text: The search reads the reasons paragraph by paragraph, so plain words find the passages where judges discuss the point: here, how non-refoulement shapes the reading of the statute.
steps.say: A legal question in plain words: non-refoulement statutory interpretation.

steps.title: The filters
steps.text: The filters sit on the left, and they all combine: outcome, court, case type, cases citing a decision, topic tags, judge, Minister and year.
steps.say: The advanced filters, starting from an empty search box.

steps.title: Outcome and court
steps.text: Outcome and court take one click each. Government won and Individual won use the outcome recorded for each decision, and several courts can be picked at once.

steps.title: Case type
steps.text: Refugee cessation (s. 108) is selected. Each group opens to its types, and the box beside a group selects every type in it. Case types come from the provisions a decision applies, worked out by fixed rules.
steps.say: Case type sorts decisions by the kind of case: here, Refugee cessation, in the Refugee protection group.

steps.title: A topic tag
steps.text: Cessation is now a filter, shown under the box; its × removes it. The list shows how many decisions carry each tag.
steps.say: Tags are the legal topics found in each decision. The first: cessation.

steps.title: A second tag
steps.text: A decision must now carry both tags, so only cessation decisions involving India remain.
steps.say: Tags combine. The second: India.

steps.title: Cases citing a decision
steps.text: Only decisions that cite Vavilov, the Supreme Court's leading case on the standard of review, are kept.
steps.say: Cases citing keeps only the decisions that cite a named case: here, Vavilov.

steps.title: Run the search
steps.text: Refugee cessation decisions tagged cessation and India, citing Vavilov, that the Minister won: five filters, one list. Words in the search box would narrow it further.
steps.say: Last, the outcome: Government won.

steps.title: The reader
steps.text: The decision as a clean document with numbered paragraphs, and what iLit found in it around the text. The reader has three parts: the header, the decision and the side panel.
steps.leadText: A refugee cessation decision, used for the rest of the tour.

steps.title: 1. The header
steps.text: Court, outcome and title, then the citation, case type, date, docket number and judge. The counts on the right are the decisions citing this one, the cases it cites and the statutes it refers to.

steps.title: 2. The decision
steps.text: The decision itself, formatted, with numbered paragraphs. Citations are marked in gold, statutes and regulations in purple, and topic tags in green; the buttons above turn each colour on or off.

steps.title: 3. The side panel
steps.text: Three tabs. About holds the outcome, case details, topics and the Outline. Authorities lists every case and statute the decision cites. Intelligence shows the judge and how this decision has been cited since.

steps.title: About
steps.text: The recorded outcome, with a link to the passage that disposes of the case, the case details, and the topics found in the text with how often each appears. Clicking a topic steps through its mentions.

steps.title: The Outline
steps.text: The decision's sections, each with the paragraph it starts at. It is marked Coming soon because section detection is not yet reliable on every decision.
steps.say: Further down the About tab is the Outline.

steps.title: Jump to a section
steps.text: The text moved to that section and marked it. In a long decision, the Outline is the quickest way to the analysis or the conclusion.
steps.say: Each section in the Outline leads into the text.

steps.title: The judge at a glance
steps.text: The Intelligence tab opens on the judge: their decisions in the library, how often the government won before them, decisions per year and the most recent ones. Open full judge profile goes further.
steps.say: The decision maker's name in the header opens the judge's snapshot.

steps.title: How it has been cited
steps.text: How many decisions cite this one and how often, the outcomes of those cases, and citing cases by year and by court.
steps.say: Beside the judge is Citation intelligence.

steps.title: A citation, previewed
steps.text: The preview names the cited case and shows the paragraph this decision points to, taken from that decision in the library.
steps.say: Back in the text: a gold citation that names a paragraph.

steps.title: Open it as a card
steps.text: The card opens under the paragraph with the cited passage in full. Its i button opens the cited case in the Intelligence tab; double-clicking the citation opens that decision in a new tab.
steps.say: A click on the citation keeps the passage open as a card.

steps.title: Pin it
steps.text: A pinned card stays open while you read on, so the passage can be checked against the reasons. Clear pinned cards, above the text, removes them all.
steps.say: The pin keeps a card open.

steps.title: A statute, previewed
steps.text: The preview shows the text of the provision, from the statute library.
steps.say: Statutes, in purple, work the same way.

steps.title: And as a card
steps.text: The card holds the provision and pins the same way. Its i button leads to statute intelligence (Coming soon), and double-clicking opens the section in the statute library.
steps.say: A click opens the provision as a card.

steps.title: Authorities
steps.text: Every case and statute the decision cites, with how many times and at which paragraphs. The arrow on a row shows the cited passage, and the filter at the top finds one quickly.
steps.say: The Authorities tab.

steps.title: Go to where it is cited
steps.text: The text moved to each place that case is cited in turn and marked it. The counter shows which one is showing, and the up arrow goes back.
steps.say: Each row steps through every place that authority is cited.

steps.title: Search this decision
steps.text: Every match is marked in the text. The arrows, or Enter, step through them, with the count beside the box.
steps.say: Search this decision finds any word in the text: here, cessation.

steps.title: Keep it on your Workbench
steps.text: The decision is now on your own list in the Workbench.
steps.writes: Saved to the demo Workbench list. It can be removed from the Workbench at any time.
steps.say: Save to Workbench keeps a decision on your own list.

steps.title: Judge profiles
steps.text: Every judge in the library is listed on the left with their number of decisions, with different spellings of a name merged into one.
steps.leadText: Judge profiles, citation intelligence and Federal Court activity.

steps.title: One judge's record
steps.text: A profile shows the judge's decisions year by year, how the cases came out, and their most cited decisions.
steps.say: The judge with the most decisions in the library.

steps.title: Citation Intelligence
steps.text: Citation Intelligence starts from one decision, here the cessation decision from the reader, and shows who relies on it: which courts and judges cite it, the outcomes of the cases citing it, and how its use has changed over the years.
steps.leadText: How one decision has been relied on since.

steps.title: Federal Court Analytics
steps.text: Built from the Federal Court's own registry of immigration files: every application for leave and judicial review as filed, including the many that end without published reasons, such as leave refused, discontinued or settled. Published case law shows only the files that reach written reasons.
steps.leadText: The Federal Court's own registry of immigration files.

steps.title: The headline figures
steps.text: The key numbers for whatever the filters select: files, how often leave and judicial review are granted, settlements, time to a leave decision, and stays of removal.

steps.title: What happens to a file
steps.text: How many filed files reach a leave decision, a hearing and a judgment, and how each year's files ended. Published decisions alone cannot show this.

steps.title: Judges and counsel
steps.text: Each dot is a judge with at least 25 leave decisions, placed by how often they grant leave and judicial review. Clicking a dot filters to that judge's files. Counsel are listed below the same way.

steps.title: Filter and explore
steps.text: Every figure now covers only files from the last five years. Further down are timing, deadlines, refusals and the decision makers under review. Rates sit beside their counts, because small groups are not reliable.
steps.say: Filters change every figure at once: for example, Last 5 years.

steps.title: Your Workbench
steps.text: The Workbench is your own space. You are signed in as Demo analyst, a demonstration account with no password; the name only keeps lists apart. Your case list follows your IMM files and flags when the Federal Court docket has moved.
steps.leadText: Your own space for cases, saved decisions and document tools.

steps.title: Your saved decision
steps.text: The cessation decision saved from the reader is here. Saved decisions take folders and notes, and Compare selected shows two side by side.

steps.title: Document tools
steps.text: Two tools work on your own documents: Live analysis reads a document against the library, and the De-identifier replaces names, ID numbers and dates with placeholders.

steps.title: Live analysis: any document
steps.text: Live analysis gives your own documents the same treatment as the decisions in the library: citations recognised and linked, statutes tied to the statute library, topics tagged. It works on a memorandum of argument, a deferral decision, an ID decision or any other Word file, text PDF or pasted text.
steps.leadText: The reader's features, applied to your own documents.

steps.title: Your document stays private
steps.text: The document is read by iLit itself, in memory, and dropped as soon as the page is drawn. It is never saved, never added to the library, and never sent to an AI model or any outside service. Closing the page leaves no copy.

steps.title: A Word file, dropped in
steps.text: A fictional Memorandum of Argument from a refugee cessation judicial review, written for this demonstration. A text PDF works the same way.
steps.say: A Word file, dropped in as it would be from a desktop.

steps.title: The memo, marked up
steps.text: The counts show the case citations and statute references found. Each one is marked in the text, and the buttons above turn each layer on or off.
steps.say: Read document runs the same rules used on the library.

steps.title: Matched to the library
steps.text: Baker is matched to the decision in the library, at the paragraphs the memo cites (21 to 28). Short forms such as 'Vavilov, above at para 99' and 'Ibid at para 100' are traced back to the case they refer to.

steps.title: Statutes, and cases not held
steps.text: IRPA and Federal Courts Act provisions are found and tied to the statute library. Cases the library does not hold are still marked, so it is clear what cannot be checked here.

steps.title: Every authority, in one table
steps.text: Each case and statute the memo cites, as written, whether the library holds it, and how often it is mentioned. Download CSV saves the table.
steps.say: One table lists every authority in the memo.

steps.title: Pull those cases in one click
steps.text: Every case in the memo that the library holds is now pinned to your list, ready to open, compare and read.
steps.writes: The library cases cited in the fictional memo were saved to the demo Workbench list. They can be removed from the Workbench at any time.
steps.say: Save library cases to Workbench pins them all at once.

steps.title: Planned: arguments and themes
steps.text: Not built yet. The next stage is argument and theme parsing. With more development, iLit should be able to identify the arguments raised in submissions, point to decisions that support or refute each one, suggest supporting citations, and flag citations that may be AI fabrications: cases that do not exist, or that do not say what they are cited for.

steps.title: The memo's cases, ready to read
steps.text: The memo's cases that the library holds are now on your Workbench, beside the decision saved earlier. Each can be opened, annotated and compared side by side.
steps.leadText: The memo's cases, now on your list.

steps.title: How the library keeps up
steps.text: A daily intake job is built. Each run checks the open A2AJ dataset for new Federal Court, Federal Court of Appeal and Supreme Court decisions, adds only the new ones through the same rule-based processing, and reads the Federal Court registry for new immigration files and docket entries. It is run by hand for now and is not yet scheduled. Refugee Appeal Division decisions are being added, with newer RPD decisions next.
steps.leadText: How new decisions reach the library.

steps.title: That is the tour
steps.text: Search and its filters, the reader, judges, citation intelligence, Federal Court analytics, the Workbench and Live analysis. The tour can be started again from the About page at any time.
